1:
Keil and Delitzsch open with the plan: the chapter contains two lamentations composed at different times, the first over the fall of Pharaoh and the second working out in elegiac form an earlier prophecy about the casting down of this imperial power. They summarise the first: the sea-monster drawn out of his waters by the net of God and cast on the earth, his flesh given to birds and beasts and the earth saturated with his blood, the lights of heaven darkened at his destruction, and the king of Babylon coming to destroy man and beast and make the land a desert. On the date Gill notes a variant, one ancient version reading the eleventh year, and Ellicott places it a year and something over six months after the fall of Jerusalem, when one great obstacle to a march on Egypt had been removed, and nearly two months after the fugitive brought the news.

Henry finds a duty in the command to lament. It concerns ministers to be much of a serious spirit and frequent in taking up lamentations for the ruin of sinners, as those who have not desired but dreaded the woeful day; and those who would affect others with the things of God must show themselves affected with the miseries sinners bring on themselves. It becomes us, he says, to weep and tremble for those who will not weep and tremble for themselves, to see whether we may set them weeping and trembling.

The comparison is double and the voices work at it. Ellicott recovers a contrast lost in the English: thou wast compared to a young lion of the nations, that is their leader and their glory, but thou wast really like a crocodile in the seas, stirring up and fouling the rivers that were the source of their prosperity; and he would render the next clause thou didst break forth in thy rivers, of the crocodile basking on the bank and plunging suddenly into the stream to stir the mud. Clarke names the two fiercest animals, on land and in the water, but suggests the second may be the hippopotamus rather than the crocodile, since there seems to be a reference to its way of feeding, walking deliberately into the water over its head and keeping on its feet while it eats the plants at the bottom, and so fouling the water with its feet. Henry reads the figures politically: great potentates, if oppressive, are in the divine account no better than beasts of prey, and a great deal of disquiet is often given to the world by the restless ambition of proud princes. Wesley glosses the rivers as armies, the waters as the neighbouring peoples and kings, and the feet as soldiers.

The net and what follows are read straightforwardly. Ellicott notes the figure of drawing the crocodile to land and casting him on the desert for food repeats an earlier chapter, and that the land wherein thou swimmest is literally the land of thine outflow, either the ground the blood is poured on or, more probably, the land of the inundations of the Nile, now to be watered with blood. Clarke explains the same phrase as Egypt, so called because intersected with canals and overflowed yearly. Gill compares the leaving on the land to a fish drawn out with a net and left gasping where it cannot live. Wesley finds a fulfilment in the deserts where the slain of the Egyptian army were left to birds and beasts; and on filling the valleys with thy height Clarke reports a rendering that gives the worms bred from the putrefaction, while Wesley reads the carcasses of the princes.
7:
Clarke turns the darkened heavens into a political key: covering the heaven is destroying the empire, the stars are the dependent states, the sun is the king himself and the moon the queen or some state less than the kingdom. Ellicott prefers a literary account, that the verse follows closely a passage spoken of Babylon and that changes in the heavenly bodies are the common prophetic figure for judgment. Wesley thinks some unusual darkness may actually have been seen about that time. Gill notes that the bright lights of heaven are, on one reading, the other five planets besides the sun and moon. Clarke also hears an older story in the setting of darkness on the land, when a former king refused to let the people go.

On the nations Ellicott prefers the marginal provoke to grief as less ambiguous, and explains that thy destruction means the news of it: the fall of Egypt was to be so striking an instance of judgment as to awaken fear in every nation that heard of it. Wesley adds that even strangers to Egypt would be troubled with apprehension of what might come on the world from so mighty a conqueror, and Clarke that remote nations with no connection to her would be amazed. Gill says their kings would fear lest their turn were next.

The quieting of the waters divides the readers sharply. Ellicott would render deep as quiet: when the restless ambition of Egypt was curbed there would come peace and quiet prosperity, and he adds that many think this a glance forward at a blessing still future, though he does not think it need look so far. Clarke reaches the same sense by his own figure, that the whole state is brought into quietness, there being no longer a political hippopotamus to foul the waters. Wesley reads the verse the opposite way, as universal sadness and heaviness, the rivers that used to flow briskly growing deep and slow. Keil and Delitzsch take sides expressly: two scholars they name understand the sinking of the waters as a diminution of the abundance of the Nile, continuing the picture of devastation, but this cannot stand, since the word introducing the sentence marks the time when the devastation has already happened; the verse contains a promise, as most commentators following two ancient authorities have rightly assumed.

Ellicott traces the same image back a step: the herds of Egypt going to the river to drink, trampling the banks and disturbing the water with their feet, stand for the restless activity of Egyptian life and its constant disturbance of the neighbouring nations, so that with the conquest all this ceases and Egypt, held within its own boundaries, is a disturber no longer. Wesley reads the same clause of depopulation, so few men left that none will trouble the water by digging or swimming or rowing, and so few beasts that none will foul it at watering time. On the closing verse Ellicott notes that the daughters of the nations is a common way of naming the nations, but peculiarly apt in a lamentation, since the formal mourning of the East was always performed by women.
17:
Ellicott dates the second dirge exactly: the month is not named, but since the previous prophecy fell in the last month of the year this must be in the same, so that just fourteen days separate them; and he says the dirge which occupies the rest of the chapter is evidently founded on a chapter of Isaiah. Clarke reports the same variant as before, that several manuscripts and one ancient version read the eleventh year. Gill says only that another prophecy of the like kind was delivered in the same year.

Henry treats the whole as a funeral we are invited to attend. The dead body of a kingdom is brought to the grave, and the prophet is ordered to cast them down as one having authority, speaking in the name of him who will do it; yet he must foretell it with an affectionate concern, wailing for the multitude of Egypt even while he casts her down. When Egypt is slain, Henry says, let her have an honourable funeral befitting her quality, buried with the daughters of the famous nations in their burying places and with the same ceremony; but he adds at once that it is a poor allay to the reproach of death to be buried with the famous, and that this is all Egypt is allowed. Shall she think to exempt herself from the common fate of proud and imperious nations? Whom does she surpass in beauty, that she should be excused when others as fair have sunk into the pit?

The command to cast them down is read as performative. Ellicott says the prophet is here, as often, told to do what he prophesies shall be done, which is a forcible way of stating that it will certainly happen; Clarke puts it as proclaiming to them a casting-down prophecy. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason: the lamentation is the word of God, and as such has the power to accomplish what it says. Gill notes that the prophet himself would not mourn but rejoice, the dirge being composed for the mourning women, and that it is said to show the certainty of the destruction. Wesley finds a sting in the burial itself, that the Egyptians affected the pyramids and their great ones would be laid apart, whereas the prophet provides them a grave among common people, buried where they fall.

The uncircumcised and the welcome from below close the section. Ellicott clears away a distraction: all question about whether the Egyptians practised circumcision is out of place, the word being simply the ordinary phrase for the heathen. Clarke presses the equality of the dead in his own way, asking how little it signifies whether a mummy is well embalmed and richly wrapped and beautifully painted, and inviting the reader to go down into the tombs and see whether one dead carcass is preferable to another. Gill gives the scene: the strongest of the mighty, famous for military exploits, generals and conquerors who could not for all their strength withstand death, are represented as meeting the king of Egypt at his grave and saluting him, taking a kind of comfort in it and insulting him as now as weak as themselves. Ellicott notes that the pronoun oscillates between masculine and feminine because the thought is partly of the king and partly of the kingdom, whichever is uppermost at the moment. Wesley says the helpers who went down before him lie there neglected and forgotten, though while they lived they bore themselves as gods.
22:
Ellicott sets the frame for the roll-call. The earlier verses gave a general picture of the fallen nations waiting to receive Egypt; now the most prominent are enumerated with a few words about each. Some were not yet fallen, he says, but in this prophetic view it is their ultimate condition that rises to the mind of the prophet: all worldly power that opposes itself to God must go down and share the judgment about to fall on Egypt. On the first named he notes that the graves of the people are set about those of their monarch, all fallen together into one common ruin. Gill and Wesley identify it as the Assyrian monarchy with its kings and soldiers, and Clarke observes that the mightiest conquerors of the earth had gone down before Egypt.

Elam gives Ellicott most trouble, and he is candid about it. Elam is substantially Persia, repeatedly conquered by Assyria and Chaldea, a warlike nation whose soldiers had long served in the Babylonian army; it was by Persian help that Assyria was overthrown and by a later union with the Medes that Babylon fell, and only after that did Persia become prominent, continuing great until the conquest by Alexander. So the prophet anticipates the future in placing Elam already in the pit, his thought looking to the ultimate result without weighing comparative dates. Ellicott allows an alternative, that Elam may be one of the nations out of whose ruin the later power arose and so already past, but he prefers the first. Clarke is briefer and less certain, placing the Elamites near the Assyrians and noting that others think Persia is meant.

The obscurer nations follow. Ellicott says it is difficult to date the fall of these smaller kingdoms, which at that period were being rapidly swallowed up by the powers contending for the empire of the world. Gill takes them for the Scythians with their armies and commanders. On the verse that seems to deny them the honours of the others, Ellicott prefers to read it as a question, which the Hebrew fully admits, rather than as a statement implying that these came to a more disgraceful end than the rest, and he glosses the closing clause as meaning that they shall die in their iniquity. Clarke explains the weapons of war as an ancient practice of burying a warrior with his arms beside him. Wesley makes the contrast sharper than Ellicott would: these leaders were not buried with the pomp of the others but, surprised by their enemies, were cut off and tumbled into pits with the rabble.

Edom and the northern princes close the list. Ellicott recalls that Edom had long since been conquered and almost destroyed, then revived to mock at the calamity of Israel, and was soon swept away herself. Wesley finds the sting exactly: the Edomites retained circumcision, being of the seed of Abraham, and it shall stand them in no stead, for they too shall lie with the uncircumcised. Clarke makes the same point by quoting verses on the equality of the dead, where those buried and unburied share an equal honour and the greatest of the Greek captains knows no more than the beggar he had condemned. On the princes of the north Ellicott notes the word differs from the one used of Edom, that one meaning the heads of tribes and this apparently implying vassal princes, and that the connection with the Sidonians shows the far north is not intended but chieftains of Syria and Damascus; he adds that Sidon had long since lost its pre-eminence among the cities of that coast but was still important and independent. Keil and Delitzsch see the prophet looking on all these smaller heathen nations with their rulers given up together to the same judgment.
